title: Tech Slump Hits Dow, S&P, Nasdaq as Oil Surges on Renewed Iran War Threat
body:
The U.S. equity market slipped on Thursday as investors grappled with a confluence of headwinds: a resurgence of geopolitical tension in the Middle East, a faltering technology sector, and rising expectations that the Federal Reserve may need to raise rates again later this year. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.5%, the S&P 500 dropped 0.7%, and the Nasdaq Composite slipped 1.1%, while the 2‑year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level in more than a year, signaling growing concerns over short‑term borrowing costs. Crude oil surged past $90 a barrel after reports that fighting in Iran could reignite, adding another layer of uncertainty to an already volatile trading day.

The market’s decline was anchored by a broad sell‑off in technology stocks, which have been the engine of growth for the S&P 500 over the past decade. Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia all posted losses, dragging the Nasdaq lower. Analysts point to a combination of factors: higher yields increasing the discount rate applied to future earnings, lingering supply‑chain disruptions, and a slowdown in consumer spending that is beginning to bite into the earnings outlook for both hardware and software firms. “Tech valuations are now more sensitive to any uptick in borrowing costs,” said Karen Liu, senior equity strategist at Meridian Capital. “When the 2‑year note spikes, the implied cost of capital rises, and investors start to reassess the premium they’re willing to pay for growth.”

At the same time, the oil market reacted sharply to intelligence that the conflict between Iran and its regional rivals could flare up again. Brent crude rose 2.3% to $91.20 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate gained 2.1% to $88.70. The price jump reflects not only the immediate threat of supply disruptions but also the broader risk‑off sentiment that typically accompanies geopolitical crises. Higher energy prices have a two‑fold impact on the broader economy: they boost revenue for oil‑related companies, which contributed modestly to the Dow’s relative resilience, but they also increase input costs for manufacturers and consumers, squeezing profit margins and discretionary spending.

The bond market’s reaction underscores the growing anxiety about monetary policy. The 2‑year Treasury yield, a bellwether for the Fed’s near‑term rate outlook, rose to 5.15%, its highest point since early 2023. This movement suggests that investors are pricing in the possibility of a second rate hike before the year’s end, after the central bank delivered a modest 25‑basis‑point increase in March. “The market is essentially betting that the Fed will not be able to achieve a soft landing without tightening further,” noted James Patel, chief economist at Horizon Analytics. “Higher yields make equities less attractive, especially growth stocks that are more sensitive to discount rates.”

The confluence of these factors has also reverberated through the currency and commodities markets. The U.S. dollar index edged higher, reflecting safe‑haven demand, while the Japanese yen and the euro slipped modestly against the greenback. Gold, traditionally a hedge against uncertainty, rose 0.8% to $1,945 an ounce, indicating that investors are seeking shelter amid the mixed signals from equities and bonds.

Looking ahead, market participants will be watching several key data releases and events for clues on the trajectory of both the economy and the conflict. The U.S. consumer price index due later this week will provide a fresh gauge of inflation pressure, while the Federal Reserve’s policy meeting minutes, expected in the coming days, could reveal whether policymakers are leaning toward a more aggressive stance. On the geopolitical front, diplomatic channels between Tehran and Washington remain under strain, and any escalation could further lift oil prices and amplify market volatility. In the short term, analysts expect continued choppiness, with technology shares likely to lead the downside unless there is a decisive shift in rate expectations or a de‑escalation of Middle‑East tensions.
